broccoli.hold_basis: M only (no crown / loose bitter heads / bolting when HEADING in heat, UMN+Iowa 86°F day/77°F night). The effect is at heading, 50-100 days after sowing, so a hot 10-day forecast at SOWING time does not predict it; G is fine to 95°F soil (UC) and UMN says heat during leafy growth is fine and directs July sowing. The only short-term heat risk T1 names is to a TRANSPLANT set out in heat (USU buttoning >85°F days/75°F nights; UC Savvy Sage: hold off transplanting in searing late-August heat), not to a sowing.
broccoli.threshold_note: 86 is the mature-plant (M) number for heat_threshold_f per climate_thresholds_contract: UMN and Iowa State both give 86°F day / 77°F night for no-crown. Matches the current value (86); no change. It is NOT a sowing-hold number. USU gives a lower growth optimum (does not exceed 75°F) and USU buttoning gives >85°F day/>75°F night for transplants.

reason_tip_candidate.field: tips_by_stage.head_forming (already carries this M reason: "heat above about 86°F by day and warm nights during heading cause bolting and loose, open heads"); if a held/advisory message is still wanted, scope it to TRANSPLANTING, e.g. tips_by_stage.seedling or start_method.notes
reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Heat hurts broccoli at heading, not at sowing: days of 86°F or more with nights of 77°F or more can stop a crown from forming. Sow the fall crop in July as usual; if you set out transplants during a hot spell, shade them from late afternoon heat until they settle in.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Hot weather is a problem when broccoli is forming its head, not when you plant the seeds. Very hot days and warm nights can keep the plant from making a head. You can still sow in summer for a fall crop; if you plant young plants out during a heat wave, give them some afternoon shade until they settle in.

gaps: No T1 source found saying broccoli seed fails to germinate or should not be SOWN during a hot spell; UC chart max is 95°F soil.
No T1 source tying a 10-day air-temperature forecast at sowing to later heading failure.
broccoli.notes: start_method=both; T1 sources (UMN, UMD, Iowa, NCSU) describe the fall crop as sown in July (or transplanted late June to early August/Sept), i.e. explicitly INTO summer heat. Evidence runs AGAINST pause_in_heat=true for a sowing. If Trevor wants a heat-time message, the defensible one is about setting out transplants (E: USU buttoning, UC Savvy Sage), which is a different action than the succession sowing the app holds. NCSU calls broccoli the most heat-tolerant brassica.

cauliflower.hold_basis: M only (curd quality/no curd/delayed curd initiation in heat at curd formation, weeks after sowing). G is fine (UC max 95°F soil; UMN: seeds germinate and plants grow well in summer temperatures) and T1 directs July sowing for fall. Short-term heat risk named by T1 is to transplants set out in heat (USU buttoning >85/75°F), not to a sowing.
cauliflower.threshold_note: For heat_threshold_f (mature-plant M number): USU "high (greater than 80°F) temperatures ... decrease head quality" and TAMU ">80°F" delays curd initiation -> 80. Current value 78 has no quote found behind it; 80 is the nearest sourced figure. Other sourced figures: TAMU 68°F daily mean for curd quality (stricter, a mean not a high), UMN/Iowa 86 day/77 night for no crown. Trevor to choose which M statistic the field encodes; none of these justifies a sowing hold.

reason_tip_candidate.field: tips_by_stage.curd_forming (already says heat causes ricing and discoloration; could add the sourced number); transplant-heat advice belongs in tips_by_stage.seedling or start_method.notes, not a sowing hold
reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Heat matters most once the curd starts: temperatures above 80°F lower head quality and can delay curd formation. Time plantings so the curd forms in cool weather; summer sowing for a fall crop is normal, but shade transplants set out in hot weather until they establish.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Cauliflower minds the heat most when the white head is forming. Days above 80°F can make the head poor or slow it down. Sowing in summer for a fall crop is normal; if you plant young plants out in hot weather, give them shade until they settle in.

gaps: No T1 source found linking riciness to a specific temperature (Iowa ties ricey to over-maturity; a 80°F riciness figure appears in an archived 1982 MSU bulletin found by search, not fetched/used).
No T1 source says not to SOW cauliflower in heat.
cauliflower.notes: start_method=both but the record itself says it is almost always transplanted. TAMU calls cauliflower "Does not tolerate heat" for mature growth; that is M, not G.

cabbage.hold_basis: M only, and weakly stated: cabbage grows best below 80°F (USU) and spring crops must be harvested before it gets too hot (Clemson). That is a season-window (last spring planting) fact, not a reason to pause one sowing for a hot 10-day forecast. G fine to 95°F soil (UC); T1 directs early-July direct seeding for fall. Splitting is a water-uptake effect (Iowa/USU/UMN/Clemson), not a heat effect; no T1 heat-bolting claim found (all T1 bolting text is cold-induced).
cabbage.threshold_note: USU: "grows best when temperatures do not exceed 80°F" -> 80, matching the current value. Note it is a growth-optimum ceiling, not a damage threshold. UC Marin gives a growth range topping at 86°F.

reason_tip_candidate.field: succession_policy.tip_seasoned (already explains the short spring window) or tips_by_stage.head_forming; no sowing-hold message
reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Cabbage grows best below about 80°F, so time spring plantings to head before summer heat. For fall, sowing in early July is standard; shade young seedlings in hot weather.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Cabbage likes it cooler than about 80°F, so get spring plants in early enough to finish before summer heat. For a fall crop, it is normal to sow in early July; give young seedlings some shade when it is hot.

gaps: No T1 source found for cabbage bolting caused by heat (Clemson, Iowa describe cold-induced bolting).
No T1 source linking head splitting to heat; all T1 sources attribute splitting to water uptake/nitrogen.
No T1 source says not to sow cabbage in a hot spell.
cabbage.notes: The brief anticipated "bolting or splitting" for cabbage; the T1 evidence does not support either as a HEAT effect. heat_effect=quality_loss is supported only by USU growth ceiling and Clemson harvest-before-hot wording.

brussels-sprouts.hold_basis: M only (bitter/loose sprouts and tipburn when sprouts MATURE in heat; USU, UMD, UC MG SCC). Sprout set is months after sowing (long-season crop), so a 10-day forecast at sowing is irrelevant to it. Crop is start_method=transplant and is not a true succession crop (record says so); T1 sows/sets it out in summer heat on purpose (Clemson Aug 15 set-out, UMN June sowing, UC IPM summer seedling shade).
brussels-sprouts.threshold_note: No T1 damage-threshold number found. USU gives a growth optimum "do not exceed 70°F" (idx 1), well below the current 78. Current 78 has no quote behind it. If the field must carry a sourced number, 70 (USU, growth-optimum) is the only one found; Trevor to rule whether a growth optimum may stand in for a stress threshold.

reason_tip_candidate.field: tips_by_stage.sprout_formation (currently has no heat reason; existing loose-sprout tip cites nitrogen only)
reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Sprouts that mature in hot, dry weather turn bitter or loose, so time plantings for sprouts to form as fall cools. Summer sowing and setting out are normal; shade summer seedlings until they have about 6 leaves.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Brussels sprouts taste best when the little sprouts grow in cool fall weather; in hot, dry weather they can turn bitter or loose. It is normal to start them in summer, so shade the young plants until they have about 6 leaves.

gaps: No T1 temperature for loose/bitter sprouts; an 80°F loose-sprout figure appears only on non-T1 sites (gardenerspath) and was not used.
No T1 source says not to SOW Brussels sprouts in heat.
brussels-sprouts.notes: Record start_method=transplant and succession tip says largely a single planting; pause_in_heat on a succession sowing barely applies. Recommend false. UMN "loose, poorly developed sprouts" is attributed to inconsistent water, not heat, so it was excluded.

kale.hold_basis: M only (bitter, tough, strong-flavored leaves when grown/harvested in heat; UMN, USU, ACES). No T1 G or sowing-in-heat failure found; T1 sows the fall crop in summer (UMN direct seed ~3 months before frost; UC Sacramento sow kale seed late August; Iowa calls kale more heat tolerant than lettuce/spinach). A hot week at sowing does not determine leaf quality at harvest weeks later.
kale.threshold_note: Only number found is USU growth optimum "does not exceed 75°F" (idx 3). Current 82 has no quote behind it. No T1 bitterness/toughness temperature found. Trevor to rule whether a growth optimum may serve as heat_threshold_f.

reason_tip_candidate.field: tips_by_stage.harvest (or established): the heat reason is a harvest-quality fact; existing established tip attributes toughness to drought only
reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Heat slows kale and turns leaves tough and strong flavored, so harvest the spring crop before hot, dry weather and keep moisture even. Summer sowing for a fall crop is normal; fall leaves sweeten as it cools.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: In hot weather kale grows slowly and its leaves get tough and bitter, so pick your spring plants before summer heat and keep them watered. It is fine to sow in summer for a fall crop.

gaps: No T1 germination maximum for kale found (UC chart has no kale row; record gives 45-85 without a located source).
No T1 temperature for kale bitterness/toughness.
No T1 source says not to sow kale in a hot spell.
kale.notes: Clemson arugula/kale/mustard/chard factsheet says "Direct seeding works well when planting in late summer for a fall harvest, when the soil is much warmer." but it sits in a general planting section, not a kale section, so it is excluded per the multi-crop rule; same wording appears on the Clemson COLLARDS factsheet (used there). Clemson's "Warm temperatures cause plants to bolt" is in the ARUGULA section, not kale; excluded.

evidence.quote: Collards are more heat-tolerant than kale or turnip greens.
Collards ( Brassica oleracea ) can be grown most of the year in South Carolina, though early spring or fall production is generally preferred.
Direct seeding works well when planting in the late summer for a fall harvest, as the soil is much warmer at this time.
If you keep the soil moist enough during hot spells in the summer, collards will produce an abundant harvest.
Plant collards in early spring for summer harvest and again in midsummer for fall and early winter harvest.

The best quality of kale or collards—flavorful, tender, non-bitter leaves—results from fast growth without heat or moisture stress. If the plants are overheated or struggling to take up water, they will produce chemicals resulting in pungent or bitter flavors.
For the spring crop, flavor is best if you harvest the plants before the weather becomes hot and dry. Heat will slow growth and leaves will become tough and strong flavored.

Other leafy greens like kale, collards, mustard, endive, and chard will be ready to harvest 8 to 10 weeks after planting in early April. These leafy greens are more heat tolerant and some may grow through the hot summer months, especially if provided enough moisture.
Direct seed again about three months before the average frost date for a fall crop.

collards.hold_basis: Weak M only (UMN: heat makes leaves tough/strong flavored, a harvest-quality effect). Strong TOL evidence: UMD most heat-tolerant of the greens, Clemson grown most of the year in SC with late-summer direct seeding in warm soil, UGA abundant harvest through summer hot spells with moisture, midsummer planting for fall. Nothing supports pausing a sowing for heat.
collards.threshold_note: No T1 heat-stress number found for collards. Current 85 has no quote behind it. UMD ranks collards above kale for heat tolerance, so a collards value at or above kale's is consistent, but no number is sourced.

reason_tip_candidate.draft_seasoned: Collards handle summer heat better than kale, and keep producing through hot spells if the soil stays moist; heat and drought together make leaves tough and strong flavored. Late-summer direct sowing into warm soil works well for fall.
reason_tip_candidate.draft_beginner: Collards put up with summer heat better than kale. Keep the soil moist in hot spells and they keep producing; hot, dry weather can make leaves tough. Sowing seeds in late summer works well for a fall crop.

gaps: No T1 temperature for collard bitterness/toughness or heat damage.
No T1 collards germination maximum (not in UC chart).
collards.notes: Evidence is clearly AGAINST a heat hold for collards; the record's own succession tip already says only extreme heat (deserts, peak FL/HI summers) warrants skipping. Clemson collards factsheet is NOT in dataset cache (fetched; saved under scratchpad/fetched).
